title: Context budgets
point: Give each prompt section a fixed token budget and evict within that section, so growth in one part never squeezes another.
definition: A context budget gives a fixed token allowance to each prompt section: system instructions, tool definitions, memory, retrieved documents, conversation history and an answer reserve. Each section evicts its own content when full, and stable sections come first for prompt caching.

objective.text: Given a context window and a cost ceiling, allocate a token budget to each prompt section, choose an eviction rule per section, and order the sections for caching.

misconceptions.claim: Fill the context window, because the model can use everything it is given.
misconceptions.correction: Every token costs money and latency, and long prompts can bury the passage that matters. Budget well below the window and spend tokens where evals show they help.

misconceptions.claim: When history grows, trim whatever is easiest, such as the retrieved documents.
misconceptions.correction: Squeezing another section degrades it silently. History summarises or drops its own oldest turns, and retrieval keeps its full allowance.

l1: Split the prompt into sections: system instructions, tool definitions, long-term memory, retrieved documents, conversation history and a reserve for the answer. Each section gets a fixed number of tokens.
When a section is full, it evicts within itself. History summarises or drops its oldest turns, retrieval keeps its highest-ranked chunks, and memory keeps its most relevant facts.
Put the sections that rarely change first, such as system instructions and tool definitions. A stable prefix can be prompt-cached, which cuts the cost and latency of repeated calls.
l2: Take a 16,000-token budget inside a 128,000-token window. Allocate 1,500 to system, 2,500 to tools, 1,000 to memory, 4,000 to retrieval, 5,000 to history and 2,000 to the answer reserve.
On turn 12 the history reaches 7,200 tokens. The history section summarises its oldest turns until it fits within 5,000, and the other five sections keep their budgets.
The first 4,000 tokens, system plus tools, are identical on every call. Placing them first lets the provider cache them, so only the later sections are processed afresh.
l3: Price the choice. At $2 per million input tokens, the 14,000-token prompt costs $0.028 per call, while filling the 128,000-token window costs $0.256, over nine times as much.
If cached tokens are billed at a tenth of the normal price, caching the 4,000 stable tokens saves the cost of 3,600 tokens per call. That is $0.0072, about a quarter of the call.
The trade-off is rigidity. A fixed budget can starve a section on unusual inputs, so measure how often each section hits its limit and rebalance from that data.
